### About the Author

Louis Auchincloss was honored in the year 2000 as a “Living Landmark” by the New York Landmarks Conservancy. During his long career he wrote more than sixty books, including the story collection Manhattan Monologues and the novel The Rector of Justin. The former president of the Academy of Arts and Letters, he resided in New York City until his death in January 2010.

Chapter 1: Brian's Journal

September 10, 1939. I have always wanted to keep a journal, but whenever I am about to start one, I am dissuaded by the idea that it is too late. I lose heart when I think of all the fascinating things I could have described had I only begun earlier. Not that my life has been an exciting one. On the contrary, it has been very dull. But a dull life in itself may be an argument for a journal. The best way for the passive man to overtake his more active brothers is to write them up. Isn't the Sun King himself just another character in Saint-Simon's chronicle?

In Europe a world war has started while in this country Brian Aspinwall is about to go to work in his first job. Surely if I am ever to keep a journal, now is the time. A first job at twenty-seven! I shall be an instructor of English at Justin Martyr, an Episcopal boys' boarding school thirty miles west of Boston. The telegram from a Mr. Ives came in only yesterday. One of the masters wants to go to Canada to enlist in the RCAF which is why I have been taken on without interviews. It makes me feel better about my rejection by the British Army before I left Oxford in July. Naturally, they were not keen about an untrained Yankee student with a heart murmur! Perhaps had I stayed over there, now that war has actually come, they might have lowered their standards, but at least this way I can feel that I am releasing an able-bodied man to fight the antichrist in Berlin.

It is the obvious moment for stock-taking. In the questionnaire that was sent out this year by my class secretary at Columbia, I had nothing to contribute but the meager fact that I had gone abroad to study for a master's degree. And now because I was too sensitive to stay in Oxford out of uniform I will not even get that! I suppose all I have basically done since my seventeenth year has been to seek refuge in literature from the agony of deciding whether or not I am qualified to be a minister. Perhaps life in a church school will help me. Please God it may.

But I must try not to be too hard on myself. That is, after all, another kind of conceit. It is a fact that I suffered all during my boyhood from ill health. It is another fact that as the only child of elderly parents I had to spend a great deal of time with them in their last illnesses. It was a joy, and I write the word sincerely, to be able to help them, but it was still time out of a career. So it is not altogether my fault that I have made so late a start; if it can be said I have even yet started.

With God's grace I shall learn my true capacities at Justin Martyr. It is a good size for a school (450 boys), and its headmaster and founder, the Reverend Francis Prescott, D.D., is probably the greatest name in New England secondary education. He is old now, nearly eighty, but he is a minister, and may have much to teach me. It may even turn out that I have been "called" to Justin.

I am shy and lack force of personality, and my stature is small. I stammer when I am nervous, and my appearance is more boyish than manly. All this will be against me. But I am not afraid to say what I mean, and I think in a real crisis I can be counted on to stand up for the right, if only because I have such a horror of letting God down. Let us hope I add up to a

teacher.

His faithful friend Brian tries to provide perspective. As the book closes, after Prescott's death, Brian is wrestling with whether his biography should include the many sides of Prescott or whether he should write it as a tribute to the man who so influenced his life.

*   ![Image 112: A 1x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://images-na.ssl-images-amazon.com/images/G/01/x-locale/common/grey-pixel.gif)  Bollard   ##### _3.0 out of 5 stars_ Upper class Marmite Reviewed in the United Kingdom on July 6, 2018 Format: Hardcover[Verified Purchase](https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html/ref=cm_cr_dp_d_rvw_avp?nodeId=G8UYX7LALQC8V9KA) Don't take my 3 stars here as gospel: the book's not to my taste, but it's a personal thing. The book won rave reviews when it was published in the US in 1964, and it was subsequently translated into a number of foreign languages. Also worth noting that Auchincloss, the author, had been brought up in the upper-crust setting he describes in much of his writing, so he knew whereof he wrote.

On the surface this is a book about Dr Prescott, who founds and leads a private (fee-paying) school in the Boston area. It's WASP territory and the school ethos is Episcopalian. The story is told via diary entries made, mostly, by Brian Aspinwall, a devotee and former student of Dr Prescott. Aspinwall is an apt name, because this character spends a lot of his time trembling like an aspen, or having fits of the vapours like a romantic heroine.

The Dr Prescott who emerges during the book is a monster, but that's just my opinion. The people who love him - in an upright, manly manner, naturally - seem incapable of forming objective views of his actions, several of which are cruel or petty. His admirers are like victims of Stockholm Syndrome: for them Dr P can do no wrong unless he himself admits it. Everyone in the book, from Dr P down, lives in the New England bubble, with little awareness of life in the real world. The Second World War, which is going on during a large part of the book, barely gets a mention. The few people who try to break out of Dr P's anal-retentive orbit suffer the consequences; others have to choose between doing things his way or taking the highway.

As the book develops, the sub-text emerges: the tension between Dr P's educational idealism and the reality of the world outside. Earlier in the book Dr P laments the fact that, despite his best efforts, most of his graduates go on to the world of business: "For all my emphasis on the humanities and his on God," says Prescott, "we both turn out stockbrokers." As one of the school's trustees puts it towards the end of the book, in a pivotal meeting where the tensions are laid bare, "It is the moral tone of the business community that sets the moral tone of the nation." In other words, in post-war America, Dr Prescott's world view, once respected, has become old hat.

Technically, this is a good book. Loath them or merely dislike them, the characters have weight. They're weird, flaky, selfish or inadequate, but they're more than stereotypes: you have good targets to aim at. The writing is a different matter. When the diary entries change from one person to another there's no change in tone or voice ... the style just carries on. And what a style! This book was published three years *after* 'Catch-22', yet it feels like a book Jane Austen could have written. True, our Dr P was born in a more slow-paced time, and perhaps that explains his use of language; but everyone else, well, seems out of time - unchanged by the fast pace of change in the US in the 20th century. (And people just don't talk like that ...) Some of the characters notice that society is changing - even Dr Prescott gets the message at the end - but it seems to make no impact upon them as individuals. Perhaps that is all part of the strange, upper-class 'bubble' they inhabit.

Overall, I felt that nothing *happened* in the whole 300+ pages. Anyone with personality, independence or character either dies, cracks up, conforms or suffers the consequences at the hands of Dr Prescott ... yet the book feels oddly static. You can see it working as a play: three hours of characters for actors to explore - that would be something. Yet on the printed page things seem cold, clinical and unlovable.

The book had rave reviews, so I'm probably being too hard on it. Yet this and Thomas Mann's 'Dr Faustus' are the only two books in my entire life that have sent me to sleep.

2.title: Louis Auchincloss
2.content:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Louis Auchincloss |
| --- |
| [![Image 1: Auchincloss receiving the National Medal of Arts from President Bush (2005)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Louis_Auchincloss_with_President_Bush.jpg/250px-Louis_Auchincloss_with_President_Bush.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louis_Auchincloss_with_President_Bush.jpg "Auchincloss receiving the National Medal of Arts from President Bush (2005)") Auchincloss receiving the [National Medal of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_Arts "National Medal of Arts") from President [Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") (2005) |
| Born | Louis Stanton Auchincloss 27 September 1917 [Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Nassau_County,_New_York "Lawrence, Nassau County, New York"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), United States |
| Died | 26 January 2010 (aged 92) [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), United States |
| Occupation | Writer, lawyer |
| Language | [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") |
| Nationality | [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans") |
| Alma mater | [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia") |
| Notable awards | [National Medal of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_Arts "National Medal of Arts") (2005) |
| Spouse | Adele Lawrence |
| Children | 3 |
| Relatives | [Nina Auchincloss Straight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Auchincloss_Straight "Nina Auchincloss Straight") (cousin) |

**Louis Stanton Auchincloss** (; September 27, 1917 – January 26, 2010)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-nytimes-1) was an American lawyer, novelist, historian, and essayist. He is best known as a novelist who parlayed his experiences into books exploring the experiences and psychology of American [polite society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_class "Upper class") and [old money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_money "Old money"). His dry, ironic works of fiction continue the tradition of [Henry James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James "Henry James") and [Edith Wharton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Wharton "Edith Wharton").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-WorldEdithWhartonnotes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-more_the_merrier-3) He wrote his novels initially under the name **Andrew Lee**,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-Clarke-4) the name of an ancestor who cursed any descendant who drank or smoked.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-5)

Born in [Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Nassau_County,_New_York "Lawrence, Nassau County, New York"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), Auchincloss was the son of Priscilla Dixon (née Stanton) and Joseph Howland Auchincloss.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-Gelderman-6) His brother was Howland Auchincloss and his paternal grandfather, John Winthrop Auchincloss, was the brother of Edgar Stirling Auchincloss (father of [James C. Auchincloss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_C._Auchincloss "James C. Auchincloss")) and Hugh Dudley Auchincloss (father of [Hugh D. Auchincloss, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_D._Auchincloss,_Jr. "Hugh D. Auchincloss, Jr.")).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-8) He grew up among the privileged people about whom he would write, although, as he put it, "There was never an Auchincloss fortune... each generation of Auchincloss men either made or married its own money".

He attended [St. Bernard's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bernard%27s_School "St. Bernard's School"), [Groton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton_School "Groton School") and [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), where he was editor of the _[Yale Literary Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale\_Literary\_Magazine "Yale Literary Magazine")_. Although he did not complete his undergraduate studies at Yale, he was admitted to and attended law school at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia"). He graduated in 1941 and was admitted to the New York bar the same year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-nytimes-1)

Auchincloss was an associate at [Sullivan & Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_%26_Cromwell "Sullivan & Cromwell") from 1941 to 1951 (with an interruption for war service from 1942 to 1945 in the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), which might have inspired his 1947 novel _The Indifferent Children_). He applied to join the Naval Reserve as an intelligence specialist on December 4, 1940 and was appointed as a lieutenant on December 1, 1942.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-9)

After taking a break to pursue full-time writing,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-10) Auchincloss returned to working as a lawyer, first as an associate (1954–58) and then as a partner (1958–86) at Hawkins, Delafield and Wood in New York City as a wills and trusts attorney, while writing at the rate of a book a year.

Auchincloss is known for his closely observed portraits of old New York and New England society. Among his books are the multi-generational sagas _The House of Five Talents_ (1960), _Portrait in Brownstone_ (1962), and _East Side Story_ (2004). _[The Rector of Justin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rector\_of\_Justin "The Rector of Justin")_ (1964) is the tale of a renowned [headmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headmaster "Headmaster") of a prep school like the one he attended, Groton School,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-11) trying to deal with changing times.

In the early 1980s, Auchincloss produced three novels which were not centered on the New York he knew so well, i.e. _The Cat and the King_, set in Louis XIV's Versailles, _Watchfires_, concerned with the American Civil War, and _Exit Lady Masham_, set in Queen Anne's England. Auchincloss would remain close to New York again, however, in his later fiction writing.

[Gore Vidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gore_Vidal "Gore Vidal") said of his work: "Of all our novelists, Auchincloss is the only one who tells us how our rulers behave in their banks and their boardrooms, their law offices and their clubs... Not since [Dreiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dreiser "Theodore Dreiser") has an American writer had so much to tell us about the role of money in our lives."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-12)

In 1957, Auchincloss married Adele Burden Lawrence (1931–1991), the daughter of Florence Irvin ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A9e "Née") Burden) Lawrence and Blake Leigh Lawrence.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-WeddingNYT-14) Her grandfather was prominent industrialist [James A. Burden Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Burden_Jr. "James A. Burden Jr.") and her great-grandmother was [Vanderbilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_family "Vanderbilt family") heiress [Emily Thorn (née Vanderbilt) Sloane White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Thorn_Vanderbilt "Emily Thorn Vanderbilt"). Adele was an artist, environmentalist and later became a deputy administrator of the [New York City Parks and Recreation Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Parks_and_Recreation_Department "New York City Parks and Recreation Department").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-AdeleObit-15) Together they had three children:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-nytimes-1)

*   Andrew Sloan Auchincloss, a lawyer who married Tracy Lee Ehrlich in 1999.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-1999Wedding-16)
*   John Winthrop Auchincloss II, a lawyer who married Dr. Tracy Pennoyer, daughter of lawyer [Robert Morgan Pennoyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Morgan_Pennoyer "Robert Morgan Pennoyer"), and sister of architect [Peter Pennoyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Pennoyer "Peter Pennoyer") (both great-grandchildren of [J.P. Morgan Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.P._Morgan_Jr. "J.P. Morgan Jr.")), in April 1988.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-1988Wedding-17)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-AdeleObit-15)
*   Blake Leigh Auchincloss, an architect[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-AdeleObit-15) who married in Lauren Stewart Moores, a daughter of John Duer Moores Jr., in June 1988.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-18)

He was president and chairman of the [Museum of the City of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_City_of_New_York "Museum of the City of New York") and chairman of the City Hall Restoration Committee and was a member of the [Century Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_Association "Century Association") and the [American Academy of Arts and Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Letters "American Academy of Arts and Letters"), where he served as president.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-nytimes-1)

On January 26, 2010, Auchincloss died from complications of a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") at [Lenox Hill Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenox_Hill_Hospital "Lenox Hill Hospital") in New York City.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-nytimes-1)

In his youth, Auchincloss was a "a [Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")-hating conservative."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-19) Once, while attending [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), he waved a sunflower (the symbol of Republican [Alf Landon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alf_Landon "Alf Landon")) at President Roosevelt's passing motorcade. Auchincloss wrote conservative articles in _[Virginia Law Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia\_Law\_Review "Virginia Law Review")_, which have been described as expressing "a nostalgic and romantic idealism".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-20)

In his adult life, Auchincloss was a registered [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-Financial-21) However, he voted for Democrat [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") explaining, "I think we're moving dangerously into a have and have not situation... for the first time in 150 years the rich are sneering at the poor."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-22)

Auchincloss described the [Bush family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_family "Bush family") as "a big family of shits." He explained his decision to receive the [National Medal of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_the_Arts "National Medal of the Arts") from President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), saying, "I didn't accept a prize from George W. Bush, I accepted a prize from the President of the United States. Who am I to turn that down?"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-Financial-21)

Significant collections of Auchincloss's papers reside at the [Albert and Shirley Small Special Collections Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_and_Shirley_Small_Special_Collections_Library "Albert and Shirley Small Special Collections Library") at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia") and at the [Beinecke Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beinecke_Library "Beinecke Library") at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"). In addition, he was the recipient of the following awards and accolades:

*   National Book Award Finalist (1960, 1961, 1965, 1967)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-23)
*   Member, [American Academy of Arts and Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Letters "American Academy of Arts and Letters") (1965)
*   Honorary degree, [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") (Litt.D., 1974)
*   Honorary degree, [Pace University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pace_University "Pace University") (1979)
*   President, American Academy of Arts and Letters (19??)
*   Honorary degree, [The University of the South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewanee:_The_University_of_the_South "Sewanee: The University of the South") (1986)
*   Fellow of the [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "American Academy of Arts and Sciences") (1997)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-AAAS-24)
*   "Living Landmark" status (2000), [New York Landmarks Conservancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Landmarks_Conservancy "New York Landmarks Conservancy")
*   [National Medal of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_Arts "National Medal of Arts") (2005)

Auchincloss wrote more than 60 books.

*   _The Indifferent Children_ (1947)
*   _Sybil_ (1952)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss#cite_note-25)

*   _The Embezzler_ (1966): National Book Award Finalist
*   _A World of Profit_ (1968) [ISBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISBN_(identifier) "ISBN (identifier)")[9789997406620](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/9789997406620 "Special:BookSources/9789997406620")
